overview: The Aikanã are a living people of Rondônia, Brazil. Their own name identifies both people and language. Older records use several other names, including Huari, which must not be confused with the distinct Wari people.

periods.title: Displacement into a restricted territory
periods.summary: In the early 1970s, land distribution and colonization displaced Aikanã families from fertile traditional lands. The new area was less productive; the sources describe a process rather than one securely agreed relocation date.

periods.title: A demarcated territory
periods.summary: Tubarão-Latundê was demarcated in 1983. Territorial recognition followed dispossession and did not restore all the places remembered by the community.

periods.title: Language teaching and cultural transmission
periods.summary: Teacher Luzia Aikanã began mother-language teaching in 1992. School work became one means of sustaining Aikanã alongside Portuguese.

items.text: Vasconcelos describes an elder making bows and different arrows for particular targets, including animals of different sizes and fish. The account records design choices connected to use. It documents a living craft observed during fieldwork, not an excavated weapon or a securely dated practice in 1492.

The Aikanã belong to a wider regional network associated with marico bags made from palm-leaf fibres. Transforming leaves into durable carrying equipment required selecting and preparing material as well as skilled construction. Shared technologies link neighbouring peoples without making their languages or identities interchangeable.

Regional food practices combine cultivated gardens, hunting and gathering. Chicha is prepared from cultivated or gathered ingredients through processing, fermentation and straining. The documentation project places these practices in a history of intercommunity contact; the regional pattern should not be read as an identical menu for every Aikanã family.

Craftwork also enters exchange with the surrounding society. Vasconcelos records ear ornaments, bracelets, necklaces, bags, rings and wooden objects being made for sale. Production for a market is part of the documented history of work and adaptation; it does not make the makers less Aikanã.

sections.title: Places, records and discoveries about language

items.text: Cascata preserves pottery remains and rock paintings near an old village and burial area, according to Grund. Aikanã memories identify it as a place of residence and meeting. These traces matter alongside oral history, but the article does not date every object or establish that all were made by one people.

Aikanã and Kwaza are distinct languages with no demonstrated membership in a larger language family. Similar grammatical features can reflect long contact between speakers. Calling a language an isolate describes what has been established about linguistic relationships; it does not mean its speakers lived without neighbours or exchange.

Aikanã speakers can link a sequence of actions while marking whether the person doing the next action changes. Van der Voort illustrates this with recorded speech and discusses exceptions in narrative use. This detailed grammar is part of the community’s intellectual heritage, rather than evidence that one language is more advanced than another.

The study prints a story told by Raimunda Dadü Kwã’ĩ at Barroso on May 6, 1996, with linguistic analysis and translation. Naming the narrator, place and recording date makes the evidence traceable. The recording date documents one performance of an older story; it does not date the story’s origin.

The DOBES project records everyday activities, personal histories, conversations and environmental knowledge, alongside word lists and grammatical work. Its multimedia record recognizes that a language lives in social use. Cooking, building and knowing plants belong in its documentation as much as isolated dictionary entries.

The 2018 teaching book Nós Kwazá Aikanã was created from cultural-mediator workshops for schools in Kwazá do Rio São Pedro. Named Aikanã and Kwazá authors and illustrators connect community knowledge with climate and territorial education. This is a concrete educational work produced with community participation.

The same book asks pupils to speak with elders, retell histories and explain pictures. Its authors describe a shared Kwazá Aikanã identity while recognizing different languages and family histories. These exercises make younger learners participants in transmission rather than passive recipients of an account written only by outsiders.

ending.text: The Aikanã continue despite epidemic losses, forced labour and dispossession. Grund’s fieldwork records living narrators preserving the history of places transformed by colonization. The map’s 1500 endpoint is not a historical disappearance or the end of the people.
